title: The tonic of wildness
hook: we need the tonic of wildness (Walden 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Walking, read again: the shortest walk, taken in the spirit of undying adventure. Your line was a new walk.

A tonic is what you take when you're run down: a bitter little bottle from the druggist's shelf, a spoonful to put color back in your cheeks. Thoreau reaches for that word in Walden's Spring chapter, after the ice has broken up and the sand bank has thawed. But his medicine doesn't come in a bottle. It comes from a marsh, a bird call, a place nobody has mapped. And he doesn't say it would be nice. He says we need it.
screen: `A BITTER LITTLE BOTTLE.` → `A SPOONFUL WHEN YOU'RE RUN DOWN.` → `THOREAU'S PRESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: The line: "We need the tonic of wildness,—to wade sometimes in marshes where the bittern and the meadow-hen lurk, and hear the booming of the snipe." First, the medicine is specific. Not nature as a postcard: wading, marshes, shy birds you hear more than see. Wildness is something you get your feet wet in. Second, two things at once: "At the same time that we are earnest to explore and learn all things, we require that all things be mysterious and unexplorable." The man who sounded the pond and surveyed fields for a living still needs places that can't be measured. Third, the limits: "We need to witness our own limits transgressed, and some life pasturing freely where we never wander." There's relief in that. Somewhere, life is going on that has nothing to do with anyone's plans or town, and seeing it puts a person back at their proper size. Fourth, wildness isn't always pretty. In the same passage he passes a dead horse near his path, the smell heavy in the air, and even there he takes comfort in nature's strong appetite and health, a world rich enough to spend lives freely. It's not a comfortable thought, but it's honest. The tonic isn't sweet, and Thoreau takes it anyway.
screen: `WADE IN THE MARSHES.` · `EXPLORE ALL, YET KEEP THE MYSTERY.` · `OUR OWN LIMITS TRANSGRESSED.` · then, large: `A BITTER TONIC.`

segments.voice: Rest your hand, or your attention, on something wild: a patch of grass, soil in a pot, a tree's bark, rain on a window, or the memory of one wild place you've stood in. Notice that it isn't yours, wasn't made for you, and is living anyway. Let that be the tonic.
The tonic of wildness. Thoreau's prescription from the Spring chapter of Walden: marshes, mystery, and life going on beyond our limits. Today's word.
Your line: wildness. Somewhere right now, life is pasturing freely where nobody wanders. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take the tonic of wildness as a reason to seek out unmanaged places, even small ones, and to let them stay mysterious.
